newsitem.title: USA: Albright appeals directly to Milosevic on elections.
newsitem.headline: Albright appeals directly to Milosevic on elections.

text.p: New U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, in a personal appeal to Slobodan Milosevic, has urged the Serbian president to ensure disputed election results are reinstated and to open a dialogue with his political opposition, the State Department said on Monday.
Her comments were contained in a letter delivered to Milosevic on Saturday by the top-ranked U.S. diplomat in Belgrade, spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

The United States remains sceptical that Milosevic will honour his pledge concerning the poll results and Albright "felt that she ought to write him personally to let her know of the strong concern of the United States on these issues," Burns said.

Albright made a point of directly communicating her views to Milosevic four days before Serbia's parliament was set to meet on Tuesday to approve a bill reinstating opposition gains in municipal elections last November.
There is speculation the legislation would reduce the already limited powers of local councils by stripping them of their sources of revenue.

But Burns warned: "The only result that will satisfy the United States is if the people who won the Nov. 17 elections actually take their seats and have sufficient powers to do their job -- meaning the powers haven't been stripped away in some back room deal, which is another option that we've heard about, another option available to the anti-democrats in Belgrade."
Results of the Nov. 17 municipal poll were annulled by Milosevic's Socialists on grounds of "irregularities," prompting weeks of domestic protests and foreign criticism.

Milosevic initially ignored the rallies that routinely drew tens of thousands of people onto the streets. But last Tuesday, apparently stung by a mounting international outcry, he said he was asking parliament to reinstate the opposition's election successes in 14 towns and cities, including Belgrade.
"The United States is looking for its quick passage and quick implementation" of the new law, Burns said.

"Our approach toward the Serbian government has remained the same and will remain the same. We expect the Serbian government to take concrete action to deal with this political crisis and to recognise the opposition victories in the Nov. 17 elections," he said.

Burns said Albright, who was sworn in to office on Jan. 23, "feels very strongly about this" and in the letter "called on Mr. Milosevic and the Serbian authorities to pass and implement quickly the elections legislation and then to open a dialogue, a formal dialogue, with the political opposition."
Albright also urged Milosevic to "take positive steps to resolve the situation in Kosovo, which has been very troubling to us and to many others in recent weeks," the spokesman said.
"And she underscored our expectation that Serbia must comply fully with the Dayton Accords, particularly with the provisions concerning war crimes."

Albright is to leave on Saturday on an 11-day tour of major European and Asian capitals. The situation in the Balkans is expected to be among the topics discussed in her talks with foreign ministers and other leaders.

Burns said he was not certain if Albright reiterated to Milosevic the long-standing U.S. view that secondary sanctions -- including American opposition to lending by international financial institutions to Serbia -- would remain in force as long as Serbia remains a repressive state.
Nevertheless, the spokesman insisted the tone of the letter was "quite tough" and Milosevic should not doubt that the secondary sanctions would remain in effect.
